title: A deployable AI-powered autonomous drone that aids search-and-rescue operations by detecting people and hazards, thereby improving responder safety and reducing victim discovery time.
description:
Background India is highly vulnerable to natural disasters including floods, cyclones,earthquakes, landslides, and flash floods, which often result in damaged infrastructure, inaccessible terrain, and delayed rescue operations. During the first few critical hours after a disaster, responders need rapid situational awareness to locate survivors, assess hazards, and prioritize rescue efforts.Traditional ground-based assessments can be slow, dangerous, and resource-intensive, particularly in remote or heavily damaged areas. Autonomous drones equipped with on-device AI can provide real-time aerial intelligence while operating in environments with limited connectivity.
Description Develop an autonomous drone system capable of navigating disaster-affected areas and performing real-time detection of survivors and hazards using on-device AI. The drone should use RGB and thermal cameras to identify stranded individuals, detect signs of human presence, and recognize environmental hazards such as fire, floodwaters, damaged structures, exposed electrical lines,debris, landslides, or chemical leaks. The solution must process data locally on the drone to ensure low latency and continued operation even when network connectivity is unavailable. The drone should autonomously map affected regions,generate situational reports, and transmit actionable insights to emergency response teams. This concept aligns with existing edge-AI drone approaches for incident response and disaster assessment.
Expected Solution The proposed solution should include some or all of the following:
• Autonomous Navigation: GPS-enabled and GPS-denied navigation capabilities using AI, SLAM, and obstacle avoidance for operation in damaged environments.
• On-Device AI Inference: Real-time detection of people, survivors, and disaster-related hazards without dependence on cloud connectivity.
• Multi-Sensor Fusion: Integration of RGB cameras, thermal cameras, IMU,and GPS sensors for accurate identification and localization of victims.
• Hazard Classification: Detection and classification of floods, fires, smoke,debris, unstable structures, landslide zones, and other safety threats.
• Geo-Tagged Mapping: Creation of live disaster maps highlighting survivor locations, hazard zones, and safe access routes for rescue teams.
• Emergency Alerting: Automatic generation of alerts and prioritized rescue recommendations based on detected risks.
• Offline Resilience: Ability to function in communication-constrained environments with optional 5G/Wi-Fi connectivity when available.
• Command Center Dashboard: Visualization of drone feeds, detected survivors, hazard markers, and mission status to support disaster management agencies.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, autonomous, drone applied to a robotics and drones problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (2/5): as a hardware build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (5/5): reaches a broad public/citizen base within Robotics and Drones. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on integration, sensor, real-time. Sustainability (2/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 22/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: A deployable AI-powered autonomous drone that aids search-and-rescue operations by detecting people and hazards, thereby improving responder safety and reducing victim discovery time.

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a drone that can fly itself through a disaster zone, spot survivors and hazards using onboard cameras (regular and thermal), and figure all of that out without needing GPS or an internet connection, because in a real disaster you often have neither.
overview.why_it_matters: In the first hours after a disaster, every minute matters for finding survivors, but ground teams are slow and put responders at risk in unstable terrain. A drone that thinks for itself on-device, with no cloud dependency, can go where it's too dangerous to send a person, immediately.
pain_points: Ground-based assessment after a disaster is slow, dangerous, and resource-intensive, especially in remote or heavily damaged terrain.
GPS is often unreliable or unavailable in disaster zones (collapsed structures, dense debris), so the drone needs GPS-denied navigation too.
Network connectivity can't be assumed, so all detection and decision-making has to happen on the drone itself, not in the cloud.
overview.background: India is highly vulnerable to floods, cyclones, earthquakes, landslides, and flash floods, which damage infrastructure and delay rescue. In the critical first hours, responders need rapid situational awareness. Autonomous drones with on-device AI can provide real-time aerial intelligence even in low-connectivity environments, aligning with existing edge-AI drone approaches for incident response.
overview.whats_being_asked: An autonomous drone system that navigates disaster-affected areas and performs real-time, on-device detection of survivors and hazards using RGB and thermal cameras, processing everything locally to work without network connectivity, then autonomously maps the region and transmits actionable insights to responders.
expected_solution: Autonomous navigation with both GPS-enabled and GPS-denied capability, using AI, SLAM, and obstacle avoidance for damaged environments.
On-device AI inference for real-time detection of people, survivors, and disaster-related hazards, no cloud dependency.
Multi-sensor fusion combining RGB, thermal, IMU, and GPS for accurate identification and localization.
Detection of environmental hazards: fire, floodwaters, damaged structures, exposed electrical lines, debris, landslides, chemical leaks.
Generation of situational reports and transmission of actionable insights to emergency response teams.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough band, correctly, because the hard part isn't any single detection model, it's making all of it (navigation, multi-sensor fusion, hazard detection, mapping) run entirely on-device with no cloud, in real conditions with degraded or absent GPS. That combination is genuinely at the edge of what's hackathon-buildable.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Autonomous navigation, multi-sensor fusion, on-device inference across multiple detection classes, and mapping/reporting are five substantial subsystems, and this is one of the few PS types where hardware (an actual drone) is non-negotiable to demonstrate credibly.

competitive_landscape.note: Disaster-response drone PS types are a perennial SIH favorite and this one is Qualcomm-sponsored with strong brand recognition, expect a large field, differentiation will come from actually flying a working demo versus a slideshow of what a drone would do.

innovation.note: Full on-device autonomous navigation plus multi-sensor hazard detection with no cloud fallback is a genuinely advanced integration, not an incremental feature.

invention.note: Five distinct subsystems (navigation, fusion, detection, GPS-denied capability, reporting) each require real engineering time.

technical_feasibility.note: Full GPS-denied SLAM navigation on a real drone in 36 hours is extremely ambitious, most credible teams will simulate navigation and focus live hardware effort on the detection/fusion pipeline.

impact_and_benefits.note: Reduced victim discovery time and responder safety in the first critical hours after a disaster is about as high-stakes an impact case as this dataset contains.

architecture.note: Navigation, sensor fusion, on-device inference, and communication/reporting all running on constrained drone hardware simultaneously is a genuinely hard systems-integration challenge.

overall_verdict.reasoning: A strong, high-impact pick, but only for a team with real hardware/robotics experience and honest scoping. Full GPS-denied autonomous navigation is unrealistic to build from scratch in 36 hours, the winning move is to demo real on-device detection (RGB+thermal fusion) on either a real or simulated flight path, and treat full SLAM navigation as an architecture description rather than a live-flown feature.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Impact and relevance are undeniable and easy to articulate to any judge, disaster search-and-rescue speed is a universally understood, high-stakes problem.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Teams without real drone hardware or flight experience risk overpromising a live autonomous flight demo that either doesn't happen or fails visibly, have a simulation or recorded-flight fallback ready from the start.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm hour 0: does the team have an actual drone platform (even a basic one) with a mountable camera, or is this being simulated? That decision reshapes the entire 36-hour plan.

idea_0_4: Decide hardware reality upfront: real drone flight demo, or on-ground/simulated detection pipeline with a recorded flight video, commit to one and build the plan around it.
If using a real drone, get camera feed (RGB + thermal if available) streaming to your on-device compute board and confirm basic connectivity before anything else.
Assign owners: one on detection models (person/hazard), one on sensor fusion/navigation logic (real or simulated), one on the reporting/mapping output.
prototype_4_22: Build the on-device person/survivor detection model first (RGB, thermal-augmented if available), this is your core deliverable and most demo-critical piece.
Add hazard detection classes (fire, water, structural damage) as a secondary detection head or separate model, prioritized by which are easiest to source training data for.
In parallel, build either the real navigation/obstacle-avoidance loop (if flying) or a convincing simulated flight-path + detection overlay (if not).
integration_22_30: Fuse RGB and thermal detection outputs into a single confidence-weighted output, and verify it runs within your on-device compute budget.
Build the situational report generation: map or annotated-image output showing detected people/hazards with locations.
Test the full pipeline against realistic disaster-scene footage or staged test scenarios, iterate on false positive/negative rates.
polish_30_36: Prepare either a live flight demo (if hardware permits) or a strong recorded-flight-plus-live-inference demo as fallback, know which one you're doing well before the deadline.
Build a clear situational-awareness dashboard showing detected hazards/people overlaid on the flight path or map.
Be ready to speak honestly about which parts (navigation vs detection) are simulated versus fully live.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: If you can't do a full live autonomous flight, don't fake it, instead run live on-device inference on a real video feed (even hand-held camera simulating drone movement) so judges see genuine real-time detection happening, that's more convincing than a scripted 'autonomous' flight that's secretly pre-programmed.

strengths: On-device detection alone (even without full autonomous navigation) is a strong, demo-able core deliverable.
weaknesses: Full GPS-denied autonomous navigation is genuinely research-grade difficulty for a 36-hour build.
Heavy dependency on physical drone hardware and flight conditions the team may not fully control at a hackathon venue.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: 2 CV/embedded-leaning to 1 backend, the detection and on-device deployment work is the technical core and the biggest time sink.
team_fit.approach: If flying real hardware, get a basic flight loop working in the first few hours as a hard go/no-go decision point, if it's not stable by hour 8-10, pivot fully to a simulated-navigation, real-detection demo rather than losing the whole build to flight debugging.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Off-the-shelf object detection model integration (person detection, basic hazard classes) and dashboard/reporting UI can be scaffolded quickly with AI assistance.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Real flight testing, sensor calibration, and false-positive/negative tuning against realistic disaster imagery need hands-on iteration, no AI shortcut replaces actually testing detection against messy, cluttered real-world scenes.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: Claiming full GPS-denied autonomous SLAM navigation was 'built' when it's actually an AI-generated code stub that was never tested on real hardware is the single biggest credibility risk for this PS, judges with any robotics background will probe this immediately.

data_resource_availability.status: Public disaster-scene and thermal imagery datasets exist (e.g. search-and-rescue, wildfire, flood detection datasets) for training/testing detection models; real GPS-denied SLAM navigation testing requires either real hardware or a robotics simulator (e.g. Gazebo, AirSim).
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If real flight testing proves unreliable at the venue, fall back to a robotics simulator for the navigation story and keep detection fully live and real on recorded or hand-held camera feed.

judge_qna.question: Did the drone actually fly autonomously, or was that scripted?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct here: state exactly what was live-flown versus simulated versus scripted, and explain why, given the 36-hour constraint, that was the right prioritization to demonstrate the core AI detection capability credibly.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would the path to full autonomous GPS-denied flight look like beyond this hackathon?

judge_qna.question: How does the system perform in smoke, dust, or heavy debris that could obscure the camera?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Thermal imaging is our primary answer to visual obstruction, we tested detection specifically under degraded visual conditions and can show the accuracy difference between RGB-only and RGB+thermal fusion.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your detection accuracy drop-off in your worst tested condition?

judge_qna.question: What happens to the data and detections if the drone loses its communication link entirely?
judge_qna.strong_answer: All detection happens on-device, so the drone continues detecting and logging locally, we'd sync/report once connectivity is restored or the drone returns to a relay point.
judge_qna.follow_up: How do you prioritize which detections to transmit first when connectivity is intermittent?
